one_liner: Maximally equidistributed 64-bit Mersenne-Twister-type generators in C; MT19937-64-class speed with optimal high-dimensional uniformity.
what_it_does: MELG-64 (Harase and Kimoto, ACM TOMS 44(3), 2018) is a family of 64-bit F2-linear generators with Mersenne prime periods from 2^607-1 to 2^44497-1, each shipped as one C file (e.g. melg19937-64/melg19937-64.c). The API copies the reference mt19937-64.c: init_genrand64(seed) or init_by_array64(key, len), then genrand64_int64(), genrand64_int63() and several double outputs (real1/2/3, res53, fast_res52), plus melg_jump() to skip 2^256 steps for disjoint parallel streams. Its selling point is quality: MELG19937-64 is maximally equidistributed (Delta = 0 versus 7820 for MT19937-64) at roughly the same speed.
how_it_is_fast: The recurrence is MT-like (312-word state for the 2^19937-1 variant) but adds one extra 64-bit state word ('lung') and a lagged tempering term, so the output is tuned for equidistribution without adding much work per word. Each call produces one word incrementally instead of regenerating the whole state block, and the index wrap-around is handled by switching a global function pointer between four specialised case functions, so the hot path has no modulo or branch on the array index. There is no SIMD path; the measured edge over reference MT19937-64 is small (about 1.06-1.21x).
when_to_use: Monte Carlo or simulation code in C that already uses the reference mt19937-64.c API and wants better high-dimensional uniformity (maximal equidistribution) at similar or slightly better speed.
Workloads that consume the most significant bits, e.g. 53-bit doubles via genrand64_res53(), where the equidistribution of leading bits matters.
Single-stream programs that need a very long period and occasional jump-ahead by 2^256 to hand out disjoint streams.
When you want to pick the state size: variants from 2^607-1 up to 2^44497-1 are provided.
when_not_to_use: Throughput is the goal: in the project's own table SFMT19937-64 with SIMD is 2.3x (Intel) and 2.2x (AMD) faster, and SFMT without SIMD is already faster on the AMD machine; a win over std::mt19937_64 was never measured.
Multi-threaded code or several generators in one process: all state is in file-scope statics, so there is one generator per program (per copy of the file).
C++ code that wants a <random> engine: there is no std::uniform_random_bit_generator wrapper.
Commercial products before the licence question is settled: LICENSE.md says MIT, but the header of melg19937-64.c restricts free use to personal, academic or non-commercial purposes.
Anything that must reproduce numbers from older copies: output values changed in 2017 (init_by_array64) and again in March 2021 (initialisation typo fix and the double output functions).

integration.dependencies: none beyond the C standard library (stdio, stdlib, math.h)
integration.min_toolchain: C99 (unsigned long long, hex float literal 0x1.0p-53); README builds with gcc -O3 -Wall
integration.platforms: any platform with a 64-bit unsigned long long; README timings on x86-64 Linux only
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe: state (melg[], melgi, lung) and the genrand64_int64 function pointer are file-scope globals; melg_jump() also rewrites that global state.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same function names and seeding API as the reference mt19937-64.c, so it can replace that file in C code, but it is not a C++ engine and its output stream differs from std::mt19937_64

gotchas: genrand64_int64 is a global function pointer that stays NULL until init_genrand64() or init_by_array64() runs; calling it before seeding is a null-pointer call.

Each .c file contains a demo main() that must be removed, there is no header, and the exported names (init_genrand64, init_by_array64, genrand64_int64, genrand64_real*) clash with mt19937-64.c if both are linked.
Use the most significant bits: the source notes the generators are optimised from the MSB down (Remark 4.1 of the paper), so taking low bits for small ranges forfeits the equidistribution guarantee.
Licence mismatch between LICENSE.md (MIT, 2021) and the source-file notice (non-commercial, contact the author for commercial use).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick MELG-64 over SFMT, VMT19937 or a faster std::mt19937_64 replacement only when maximal equidistribution of 64-bit outputs is the requirement and MT-class speed is enough; for raw throughput SFMT with SIMD (same table) or VMT19937's vectorised MT19937-64 are the better choices.
verified_claims_summary: The README reports CPU time for 10^9 64-bit outputs with gcc -O3 on Linux (compiler version not given): 4.21 s on an Intel Core i7-3770 and 6.29 s on an AMD Phenom II X6 1045T, versus 5.10 s and 6.65 s for the reference mt19937-64.c (about 1.21x and 1.06x faster), 4.27 s and 5.61 s for SFMT19937-64 without SIMD, and 1.85 s and 2.88 s with SIMD. These are first-party numbers with no timing harness in the repo, and std::mt19937_64 itself was not measured.
status_note: Abandoned research code (last commit 2023-03-18, 3 issues all closed) that is small enough to vendor, but check the MIT-versus-non-commercial licence conflict first.
